title: The Safavid Empire
description: An illustrated map of the Safavid Empire, from the Sufi shrine at Ardabil and Ismail’s crowning at Tabriz through Chaldiran, the Ardabil carpet and Humayun’s exile, to Shah Abbas’s Isfahan, the Armenians of New Julfa, Hormuz and Baghdad, the Afghan siege of 1722 and Nader Shah’s crowning on the Mughan plain.
mapLabel: Illustrated map of the Safavid Empire, from about 1301 to today
note: Based mainly on Safavid court histories (above all Iskandar Beg Munshi’s History of Shah Abbas), on Ottoman and Mughal sources, on European travellers and East India Company records, and on surviving buildings and works of art; each chapter says which it follows. Court histories praise the shahs, and travellers’ numbers for people and armies are guesses. Kandahar lies beyond the map’s eastern edge, so routes run off the map from it. Native names are given in Persian. The map is stylised and not to scale. Lands under Powers are painted loosely.

steps.title: The Sufis of Ardabil
steps.text: At Ardabil, Sheikh Safi al-Din leads a Sufi order (a mystical brotherhood) from 1301 until his death in 1334, and his tomb becomes its shrine. His descendants, the Safavids, turn the order into a fighting movement, followed by Turkmen tribesmen called Qizilbash, “red heads”, from their red caps. Two of its sheikhs, Junayd and Haydar, die in battle.
steps.today: Today: Ardabil, Iran. The shrine of Sheikh Safi al-Din is a World Heritage Site.

steps.title: Ismail crowned at Tabriz
steps.text: In 1501 Ismail, the fourteen-year-old head of the order, defeats the Aq Qoyunlu (White Sheep) Turkmen, takes Tabriz and is crowned shah. He declares Twelver Shia Islam the faith of his realm, though most Iranians are then Sunni; conversion takes generations and is sometimes forced. By 1510 he holds almost all of Iran.
steps.today: Today: Tabriz, Iran. Its covered bazaar, one of the oldest in the Middle East, is a World Heritage Site.

steps.title: Chaldiran
steps.text: The Sunni Ottoman sultan Selim I sees the Shia shah as a threat and marches east. At Chaldiran in August 1514 his janissaries, with muskets and cannon behind a wall of carts, rout the Qizilbash cavalry; Selim briefly holds Tabriz. Ismail is said never to have led an army again. The empires fight on and off for a century.
steps.today: Today: the plain near Siah Cheshmeh (Chaldoran), West Azerbaijan province, Iran, close to the Turkish border.

steps.title: The Ardabil carpet
steps.text: Shah Tahmasp, Ismail’s son, is a great patron of painting and weaving in his youth. A pair of huge carpets, dated 1539–40 and signed by Maqsud of Kashan, is said to have been woven for the family shrine at Ardabil. Court painters also make a vast Shahnameh (Book of Kings), with 258 paintings, among the finest Persian manuscripts.
steps.today: Today: one of the pair is in the Victoria and Albert Museum, London, the other in the Los Angeles County Museum of Art.

steps.title: A Mughal emperor’s refuge
steps.text: In 1544 the Mughal emperor Humayun, driven out of India by Sher Shah Suri, reaches Tahmasp’s court as a refugee. Tahmasp gives him troops to win back Kandahar and Kabul. Persian painters, Mir Sayyid Ali and Abd al-Samad, later join Humayun and help found Mughal painting. To be further from the Ottomans, Tahmasp moves his capital to Qazvin.
steps.today: Today: Qazvin, Iran. The Chehel Sotoun pavilion survives from Tahmasp’s palace gardens.

steps.title: Half the world
steps.text: Shah Abbas I makes Isfahan his capital in 1598 and builds round the Naqsh-e Jahan square, about half a kilometre long, the Shah Mosque, the Sheikh Lotfollah Mosque, the Ali Qapu palace gate and the royal bazaar. A saying calls the city “half the world”. He curbs the Qizilbash with a new army of converted Georgian, Armenian and Circassian slaves.
steps.today: Today: Isfahan, Iran. Naqsh-e Jahan Square is a World Heritage Site.

steps.title: The shah walks to Mashhad
steps.text: Abbas wins back Mashhad from the Uzbeks in 1598, and in 1601 walks there from Isfahan on pilgrimage to the shrine of Imam Reza, the eighth Shia imam, a journey of nearly 1,000 km. With the shrines of Iraq in Ottoman hands, he makes Mashhad Iran’s great Shia pilgrimage city and endows it richly.
steps.today: Today: Mashhad, Iran’s second-largest city, grown round the shrine of Imam Reza.

steps.title: The Armenians of Julfa
steps.text: At war with the Ottomans, Abbas lays waste his own north-western frontier so that an invader finds nothing. The Armenians of Julfa, a rich town of merchants on the Aras river, are forced to move to Isfahan, and many die on the way. Settled in New Julfa, beside the capital, they run a silk trade reaching from Europe to India.
steps.today: Today: New Julfa is still Isfahan’s Armenian quarter, with the Vank Cathedral. Old Julfa’s carved-stone cemetery was destroyed between 1998 and 2006.

steps.title: Hormuz taken
steps.text: The Portuguese have held the island of Hormuz, at the mouth of the Gulf, since 1515. In 1622 Abbas’s army, carried and supported by ships of the English East India Company, besieges and takes it. Trade moves to a port on the mainland, Bandar Abbas, “Abbas’s harbour”, where English and Dutch merchants set up their trading posts.
steps.today: Today: Hormuz Island, Hormozgan province, Iran, where the ruins of the Portuguese fort still stand.

steps.title: Baghdad won and lost
steps.text: In 1623 Abbas takes Baghdad from the Ottomans, with the Shia shrines of Najaf and Karbala. He dies in 1629. In 1638 the Ottoman sultan Murad IV retakes the city, and the Treaty of Zuhab in 1639 fixes a frontier close to today’s border between Iran and Iraq. Iraq stays Ottoman until the First World War.
steps.today: Today: Baghdad, Iraq. Zuhab lay near Qasr-e Shirin, on today’s Iran–Iraq border.

steps.title: Travellers in Isfahan
steps.text: Under Abbas II, Isfahan keeps growing: the Chehel Sotoun palace and the Khaju bridge, with its terraces over the river, date from his reign. European travellers come to trade and write. The French jeweller Jean Chardin, who lived here for years, compared Isfahan in size with London; his population figures, like most travellers’, are guesses.
steps.today: Today: Isfahan. The Khaju and Si-o-se-pol bridges still cross the Zayandeh river, which now often runs dry.

steps.title: The siege of Isfahan
steps.text: Ghilzai Afghans, rebels from Kandahar led by Mahmud Hotak, defeat the Safavid army at Gulnabad in March 1722 and besiege Isfahan. Famine kills many thousands in the city; the number is uncertain. In October the shah, Sultan Husayn, surrenders and hands Mahmud his crown. Ottoman and Russian armies then seize Iran’s western and northern provinces.
steps.today: Today: Gulnabad, where the battle was fought, is a village east of Isfahan.

steps.title: Nader takes the crown
steps.text: Tahmasp II, a son of Sultan Husayn, wins back Isfahan in 1729 with his general Nader, who deposes him in 1732. In March 1736, at a great gathering on the Mughan plain, Nader has himself proclaimed shah, and Safavid rule ends. In 1739 he sacks Delhi and carries off the Mughal Peacock Throne.
steps.today: Today: the Mughan plain, on the Aras river along the Iran–Azerbaijan border.

steps.title: A Shia nation
steps.text: Safavid rule made Iran a mainly Shia country, as it remains, with the largest Twelver Shia population in the world. The shahs’ Isfahan set a style of tilework, gardens and bridges copied across Iran. Nader Shah, who had ended the dynasty, made Mashhad his capital and is buried there. The Safavid frontier with the Ottomans still divides Iran and Iraq.
steps.today: Today: Mashhad. Nader Shah’s tomb, rebuilt in the 1950s, stands in a garden in the city.

items.name: Safi al-Din
items.text: A disciple and son-in-law of the Sufi master Zahed Gilani, Safi al-Din led his order from Ardabil for over thirty years, with followers across Anatolia and Iran. Whether he and his early followers were Sunni or Shia is debated; later Safavid histories rewrote his story to give him a Shia, and royal, ancestry.

items.name: Ismail I
items.text: Ismail was a boy when he took the throne and a poet all his life, writing in Turkish under the name Khata’i. In his poems he speaks of himself in near-divine terms, and his Qizilbash followers revered him as more than a king. His choice of Shia Islam shaped Iran ever after.

items.name: Tahmasp I
items.text: Tahmasp came to the throne at ten and reigned fifty-two years, the longest of any Safavid. In youth he painted and paid for some of the finest Persian books; later, growing strictly pious, he turned away from painting, and several court artists left for the Mughal court. He also wrote a short memoir.

items.name: Humayun
items.text: Humayun, son of Babur, lost India to Sher Shah Suri in 1540 and spent fifteen years in exile. With Persian help he took Kandahar and Kabul, and in 1555 won back Delhi, only to die the next year after falling down the stairs of his library. His son Akbar was born during his flight.

items.name: Abbas I
items.text: Abbas I took the throne at sixteen amid civil war and invasion, and won back Iran’s lost lands from Uzbeks and Ottomans. He built a standing army with muskets and cannon, and built Isfahan and roads lined with caravanserais. He could be ruthless: fearing plots, he had one son killed and two others blinded.

items.name: Jean Chardin
items.text: A Paris jeweller’s son who travelled to Iran to sell jewels to the shah and stayed for years, learning Persian. His Travels in Persia, published in 1686 and 1711, are one of the fullest European accounts of Safavid life. A Protestant, he settled in London, where he was knighted.

items.name: Mahmud Hotak
items.text: Mahmud Hotak was the son of Mirwais, a Ghilzai chief who had rebelled against Safavid rule in Kandahar. After taking Isfahan he ruled as shah for about three years, growing ever more violent and unstable. He was overthrown and killed in 1725 by his cousin Ashraf.

items.name: Nader Shah
items.text: Nader rose from a humble family of the Afshar Turkmen tribe to become the greatest general of his age. As shah he invaded India and sacked Delhi, and fought Ottomans, Afghans and Uzbeks. He grew cruel and suspicious in later years and was murdered by his own officers in 1747.
